name: Martin of Tours
knownFor: A Roman soldier who asked to leave the army as "Christ's soldier", became a monk and then bishop of Tours without ceasing to live as a monk, and at Trier begged that no blood be shed over Priscillian's heresy, saying a judge of this world should not try a case of the church.
dates: Fourth century. Sulpicius Severus gives no years. Ernest Brehaut, the translator of Gregory of Tours, dates his death to 8 November 397; Gregory gives 11 November as the day of his burial. Gregory says he was born in the eleventh year of Constantine and died in the eighty-first year of his life, but those figures do not fit Sulpicius's account of his years in the army
place: Born at Sabaria in Pannonia, in what is now Hungary; raised at Ticinum (Pavia) in Italy; a monastery near Poitiers; bishop at Tours, on the Loire, in Roman Gaul; died at Candes, a village of his diocese
role: Soldier, monk and bishop of Tours

traces: Monastic houses in Gaul. Sulpicius Severus tells of a monastery near Poitiers and another two miles outside Tours, between a cliff and the Loire, where eighty disciples joined him. He says many of those monks were later made bishops, and that cities wanted their priests from Martin's monastery. Edgar Gibson, who translated John Cassian, names the houses Ligugé, founded shortly after 360, and Marmoutier, after 371; Sulpicius does not name them.

His tomb at Tours. Gregory of Tours says Perpetuus, the fifth bishop after Martin, built a great church over the grave because miracles were reported there, and told the faithful to keep a July feast for the church's dedication, the moving of Martin's body and his ordination, and to remember his burial on 11 November. Brehaut calls Tours "the chief point of Christian pilgrimage in Gaul."

The Life by Sulpicius Severus. Sulpicius claims, through a speaker in his Dialogues, that it sold fast in Rome and was read in Carthage, Alexandria and the Egyptian desert. Brehaut says it "became a model for saints' lives" and calls Gregory's own Miracles of Martin "merely a continuation of it." Venantius Fortunatus put it into verse in four books, writing that "a soldier's white cloak is more than a king's purple".
remembered: At his funeral, it was said, almost two thousand monks gathered.

Gregory of Tours calls him "our blessed patron Martin". He says Clovis ordered his army to take nothing but grass and water from Martin's lands, brought gifts to Martin's church after his victory, and put on a consul's purple there.

In Sulpicius's Dialogues, one of Martin's own monks tells how Martin, to save men condemned to die, shared communion for one day with the bishops of Ithacius's party but refused to sign his name to it. He grieved over it, and "never again did he attend a synod."

Gregory of Tours, at a council in Paris where other bishops sat silent before King Chilperic, reminded them that Maximus had forced Martin to yield, and that "the judgment of the eternal King pursued him" until he lost his throne and his life. Gregory's point is the punishment of Maximus; the principle that no worldly judge should try a church case rests on Sulpicius alone.

Gregory of Tours, writing nearly two centuries later, says the people of Poitiers and of Tours quarreled over his body at Candes, and that the people of Tours carried it home by night on the river. Sulpicius's account of the funeral says nothing of this.

uncertain: Almost everything known of him comes from one admirer, Sulpicius Severus, whose Life is a saint's life full of miracles. Sulpicius met Martin late in life, visited him and questioned him, and published the Life while Martin still lived. For most events he was not present and relied on Martin and on "those who had lived with him"; for the death he relied on those who were there. Sulpicius swears he wrote "nothing of which I had not certain knowledge and evidence." Alexander Roberts, his English translator, says it is "extremely difficult to decide as to the real value of his narrative."

The dream of Christ wearing the half-cloak, and the surrender of the enemy the day after Martin offered to stand unarmed, are Sulpicius's telling. That the peace was Martin's victory is Sulpicius's own reading.

Sulpicius is on Martin's side at Trier. In his Chronicle he calls Ithacius "a bold, loquacious, impudent, and extravagant man." He also says that "the accusers were as distasteful to me as the accused." Martin did not defend Priscillian's teaching; he accepted the bishops' verdict and asked only that the condemned be cast out of the churches, not killed.

Roberts's English of the Chronicle says the trial was put off "as long as Martin survived". Halm's Latin says it was put off while Martin was at Trier, and that he won Maximus's promise as he was about to leave. Martin was alive when Priscillian was put to death: the Dialogues have him back at Trier afterwards. The brief follows the Latin. Roberts's "foul" renders saeuum, "cruel"; one early edition reads nouum, "new".

The three accounts of Trier differ. The Chronicle has Martin delay the trial and win a promise, with no yielding. Sulpicius's Dialogues have a later visit at which he shared communion once to save lives. Gregory says Maximus "forced" him and that he "yielded". The Dialogues say he lived sixteen years after that day, which fits poorly with a death in 397.

Sulpicius gives no years for Martin's life. Gregory's birth year and age at death would make Martin much older than Sulpicius's figures allow when he left the army (sworn in at fifteen, baptised at twenty, nearly two more years of service). Brehaut dates the Life to about 400, but Sulpicius's letters show it was published while Martin lived.
Sulpicius places the cloak at the gate of the city of the Ambiani, which Roberts says "is supposed to be the modern Amiens." He does not name the monastery near Poitiers.

Sulpicius says Martin fell ill on a peace-making visit to the church at Condate, which Roberts thinks is probably Cosne. Gregory of Tours places the illness and death at Candes, a village of his diocese.
No writing by Martin himself survives in these files. Every word of his is reported by Sulpicius.

briefReferences: Sulpicius, Life 2, tr. Alexander Roberts: born at Sabaria in Pannonia to heathen parents; a catechumen at ten; seized, chained and sworn in at fifteen on his father's information.
Life 3: the cloak at the gate of Amiens in a winter fatal to many; the onlookers who laughed and those who groaned. The dream of Christ in the half-cloak, told as a vision in sleep.
Life 3: baptised at twenty; nearly two more years in the army for his tribune's sake.

Life 4: the donative of the Caesar Julian, the request for discharge, the charge of cowardice, the offer to stand unarmed, prison, the enemy's surrender, and Sulpicius's "who can doubt that this victory was due to the saintly man?"
Life 5 and 7: to Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; the monastery not far from the town.
Life 9: Ruricius and the pretended sick wife; the crowds and "a kind of guard".
Life 10: a bishop who kept a monk's life; the wooden cell two miles outside Tours, by the Loire; eighty disciples. Life 10 also: many of his monks made bishops.
Life 25: Sulpicius's journey to see and question him.
Chronicle II.50 (Latin, ed. Karl Halm, and Roberts's English): Martin at Trier, his plea for the condemned and against a secular judge; the trial delayed while he was there; the deaths after he left.
Dialogue III.11–13: the later visit; communion shared for one day to save lives; his refusal to sign.
Epistle III: almost two thousand monks at his funeral, as it was said.
Dialogue I (Postumianus): the Life sold in Rome and read in Carthage, Alexandria and Egypt, as Sulpicius claims.
Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, tr. Ernest Brehaut: Perpetuus's great church over the tomb; Clovis's edict on Martin's lands; Gregory's words at the council in Paris on Maximus and Martin.
World census, Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity ("The Monk-Bishops of Gaul"): his setting and tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: I am Christ's soldier. I am not allowed to fight.
quotationOriginals.printed: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.
quotationOriginals.original: Christi ego miles sum: pugnare mihi non licet.
quotationOriginals.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St. Martin 4; English tr. Alexander Roberts, Latin ed. Karl Halm
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Halm's Latin, not Roberts's English. The OCR reads "miles snm" for "miles sum".

quotationOriginals.modern: it was a cruel wrong, never heard of before, for a judge of this world to try a case of the church.
quotationOriginals.printed: it was, besides, a foul and unheard-of indignity, that a secular ruler should be judge in an ecclesiastical cause.
quotationOriginals.original: saeuum esse et inauditum nefas, ut causam ecclesiae iudex saeculi iudicaret.
quotationOriginals.work: Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.50, Martin's words as Sulpicius reports them; English tr. Alexander Roberts, Latin ed. Karl Halm
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Halm's Latin, not Roberts's English. "cruel" follows saeuum, the reading of the main manuscript P (OCR "saeunm"; apparatus "Beanm P"); an early edition reads nouum, "new". Roberts's "foul" is loose. The next sentence of Roberts's English mistranslates the Latin; see the uncertainties.
